2610.40685.title: Agentic Systems for Calibrating Cosmological Simulations

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Agen$t$icTuner. At each step t, the agent can observe the workspace $o_{t,i}$ or run a low-resolution probe before submitting $\theta_{t+1}$ to the simulator $\mathcal{M}$. If the trial converges, the loop terminates; otherwise, the agent’s context is cleared, and the loop restarts with the updated $\mathcal{D}_{t}$.

Figure 2: Reduced-$\tilde{\chi}^{2}$ vs. trial number for AgenticTuner (teal) and BO baseline (orange). We present ten representative runs from our 20 experiments for legibility. To stress test our algorithm, we reduced the allowed CPU budget for both methods in the bottom row, which explains the total lack of convergence in BO runs.

Figure 3: Per-invocation timeline of AgenticTuner ’s reasoning and tool calls, early vs. late in the run (pooled over independent runs; five shown per panel to save space). Actions are fetched and classified from the saved traces; Other covers miscellaneous sanity-check code. Legend percentages (early/late) give each action’s total share across all runs.

Figure 4: Per-trial parameter-recovery error $|\theta-\theta_{\rm fid}|/({\rm hi}-{\rm lo})$ across two representative converged AgenticTuner runs; colored curves are the parameters the agent chose to tune.

2610.40685.abstract: Calibrating a cosmological simulation is an expensive, high-dimensional parameter optimization task. Previous works employ Bayesian optimization for automation, which treats the simulator as a black box and precludes the incorporation of human domain knowledge or workflow into the selection policy. We propose AgenticTuner, an agentic calibration pipeline with a present-day large language model serving as the optimizer who proposes the next parameter trial. We show that these agents can achieve competitive calibration performance at a fraction of the CPU cost when they are given informal, human-readable priors (such as codebase, documentation, and heuristic guides that seasoned scientists may possess). We hope this work serves as an early step toward AI scientists that can carry out complex, long-horizon scientific tasks.

2610.41071.title: An Assessment of Water Vapor Radiometry Landscape in ngVLA Context

figures.caption: Figure 1: : NOEMA WVR performance in the 3-mm band. The distribution of raw uncorrected phases (top row) and that of WVR corrected phases (bottom row) are shown for different PWV conditions. The computed coherence factor per baseline for the median phase error is listed in red in each panel. The bottom row includes the coherence factor after correction, the achieved improvement in the coherence factor, and the fraction of data that gained improvement. The comparison is shown on a lab stability test plot of the prototype CWVR (Allan Standard Deviation; $\sigma$ normalized by mean power $\mu$ for WVR channel i), adapted from [10]. 2610.41071.abstract: The ngVLA intends to utilize Water Vapor Radiometry (WVR) as an approach to lower calibration overheads for tropospheric phase fluctuation correction in its high frequency bands (5 \& 6; 30.5-116 GHz) to levels below those feasible with fast switched reference gain calibration. As a stepping stone to an eventual ngVLA WVR system, the JVLA/ngVLA teams pursued an effort to develop and install a set of MMIC based compact water vapor radiometers (CWVR) and carry out on-sky testing. Most recent tests found that the CWVRs installed on the VLA antennas under this effort were non-functional in tracking visibility phases. As part of the program to develop a WVR system for the ngVLA, this memo summarizes the current landscape of water vapor radiometry experience, the situation with the CWVRs, how they relate to the ngVLA WVR requirements, and the work needed to operationalize the CWVRs as useful test systems and to make broader progress. We currently lack statistically relevant WVR correction data to understand their expected performance for the ngVLA sites. We also discuss parallel additional approaches alternative and/or complementary to the CWVRs. A path involving tests to establish the functionality, stability, sensitivity, and switched power cal/data synchronism of the CWVR system in the lab and on antenna, followed by on-sky tests, and a parallel effort to assess the utility of autocorrelation outputs of the VLA K-band receivers for delay estimation is recommended. Potential paths going beyond traditional excess path estimation methods which may be necessary to meet ngVLA requirements and goals are touched upon.

2610.41092.abstract: High-resolution optical imaging is fundamentally limited by diffraction, which imprints wavelength-dependent structure onto the point spread function (PSF) of the optical system. This intrinsic chromaticity implies that in addition to spatial structure, images encode spectral information. We develop the theory of this spectral information content and provide strategies for its optimal extraction with calculations of Fisher information. We show that polychromatic PSF formation can be expressed as a convolution in logarithmic coordinates and define the corresponding spectral transfer function. We derive this function for the Airy disk and find algebraic decay in spectral log-frequency, implying the existence of arbitrarily fine spectral structure in the ideal, noiseless PSF. We use a differentiable forward model to numerically construct the spectral information eigenbasis and quantify the spectroscopic capability of diffraction-limited imaging across a range of noise and detector systematics. We demonstrate injection and recovery of the constrained spectral modes in a realistic simulated example and compare these results with previously reported methods. Our information-theoretic framework provides a generalisable method for spectral characterisation of PSFs spanning a variety of imaging contexts.

2610.41481.abstract:
Several near-infrared instruments on upcoming extremely large telescopes use a combination of OHARA S-FPL51 and S-LAH71 glass prisms to correct for the atmospheric differential refraction. Because large parts of these instruments are contained within a vessel cooled to liquid nitrogen temperatures, the changes in optical and mechanical properties should be considered during the design phase.
In this report, we provide an update to our continuing efforts to characterize the S-FPL51 and S-LAH71 glass under cryogenic conditions. These efforts include a measurement of the refractive index (293 K, 100 K and 80 K), transmission measurements (293 K, 77 K and 43 K) and a determination of the coefficient of thermal expansion (between 293 K and 45 K). We will describe the cryogenic test setups that we have used to obtain our results, and provide summarizing equations of these material properties.
This characterization will prove useful for conceptual design trade-offs, mechanical interface solutions and detailed optical design for future near-infrared instrumentation on large telescopes.

2610.41535.abstract: This paper presents the demographics and growth of the astronomy and astrophysics community over the past ~200 years based on data provided by the Astrophysics Data System. The analysis suggests that 59940 authors signed at least one paper in 2025, while about 40% of the community did not publish any papers, resulting in an estimated community size of roughly 100000 astronomers in 2025. About 38% of the community is hosted in Europe, followed by Asia (29%), North America (26%), South America (4%), Oceania (2%) and Africa (1%). Large variations exist among the countries in the number of astronomers, astronomers per capita of country population and astronomers per country gross domestic product (GDP). Overall, the community is dominated by early career scientists, with 50% of the authors publishing papers for seven years or less. This dominance is readily explained by a steady and exponential growth of the community of 4.3% per year over the last 50 years, implying that the community-size doubled every 16 years. The growth rate of the community exceeds that of the number of papers or paper pages, implying that the annual number of papers or pages published per astronomer is on decline. Over the last decade, the exponential growth of the community has accelerated to 5.1% per year, owing in particular to countries like China (13% per year) and India (10% per year). For almost all countries in the world, growth rates in authors, authors per capita and authors per GDP are positive. The growth in astronomy is not an exception, as the growth rates of the earth sciences and physics communities are even larger. If the past tendencies continue, Chinese and Indian astronomers will be first and second largest communities in the world by 2029 and 2043, respectively.

2610.41586.abstract: We investigate the optical response of a rotating sapphire half-wave plate (HWP) with optic axis misalignment, defined as a deviation of the optic axis from the ideal a-cut orientation. We extend the transfer-matrix formalism for calculating the modulated transmittance of multi-layer wave plates with optic axis misalignment and oblique incidence. Using this formalism, we compute the modulated response of a rotating HWP with an optic axis misalignment to linearly polarized incident light. We experimentally validate the model at 90 GHz using sapphire wave plates with intentionally introduced optic axis misalignments of up to 30 degrees. Additional even harmonics are observed for oblique incidence and optic axis misalignment, with odd harmonics appearing when both effects are present. The measured modulation signals are in good agreement with the model predictions. We also evaluate the potential impact of a illustrative small optic axis misalignment of 3 degrees on precision polarimetry. For the configuration considered, the model predicts odd-harmonic amplitudes at the percent level for a single-layer HWP and up to 8% at individual frequencies for a five-layer achromatic HWP.

2610.41775.abstract: Dark100 is the first phase of an extensive array of Panoramic SETI (PANOSETI) telescopes at Palomar Observatory, California. PANOSETI telescopes are small, 0.5-m Fresnel lens telescopes instrumented with 1024-pixel silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) cameras. The telescopes were originally designed to search for ultra-fast optical transients, but they also function as cost-effective imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (IACTs). Dark100 will use seven of these widely separated IACTs to map the ultra-high-energy (UHE) gamma-ray sources on the Galactic Plane at high resolution. Dark100 will also leverage the IACT technique to search for evidence of ultra-heavy dark matter in a mass range that extends beyond 100 TeV. Deployment of the first four telescopes and enclosures was completed in December 2025, and commissioning of the next three is scheduled to finish by the end of 2026. The array has so far collected more than 100 hours of 3-telescope data on sources including the Crab Nebula and Markarian 421. Here we present the current status of Dark100.

2610.41934.title: An exploration of in-band spectral index techniques for extended radio sources with EMU

figures.caption: Figure 2: Images of Cen B. Here we show Stokes I from EMU at 943 MHz (left), the sub-band spectral index map (middle), and the Taylor term spectral index map (right).

Figure 3: Sample sub-band spectral index maps for six of the H II regions studied. We can see a mix of optically thin (flat) components and optically thick (steep positive) components. We often find small bright optically thick cores surrounded by optically thin emission. These sources will have overall indices that are an average of these components. Steep negative edges can be seen in some of the sources, corresponding with regions where the emission becomes fainter and the indices are less reliable.

2610.41934.abstract: Spectral indices are an effective way of differentiating between thermal and nonthermal sources of radio emission. Most often, spectral indices are determined using flux measurements taken over multiple observations with different instruments. Since these data are not always available, determining spectral indices from a single telescope observation is desirable. The reliability of these in-band spectral indices has not been well studied, particularly for extended sources. Here, we explore three different techniques for finding in-band spectral indices with the Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU), a radio southern sky survey being conducted with the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP). These methods include: (1) integrating fluxes in sub-bands, (2) temperature-temperature (T-T) plots, and (3) using the ratio of the Taylor terms produced in the imaging process. We apply these techniques to a selection of extended sources of radio emission, primarily supernova remnants (SNRs) and HII regions, and assess if the indices produced through these methods agree with the expected values. For the SNRs, we also compare the in-band results to broadband spectral indices determined using flux values obtained from published works. We examine whether and when the in-band techniques can differentiate between thermal and nonthermal sources. In general, we find the T-T plot method to be the most reliable across the range of source sizes and brightnesses studied for both SNRs and HII regions. The sub-band and Taylor term methods can be useful under certain conditions but cannot be considered as broadly reliable for extended sources.

2610.40958.title: Optimizing Prompt Radio Counterpart Searches for Gravitational-Wave Events with the Deep Synoptic Array

figures.caption: F$i$gure 1:  Representative simulated BNS localization sequence used in the follow-up environment. The injection has component masses $1.28+1.83\,M_{\odot}$, a luminosity distance of $D_{L}\simeq 93$ Mpc, and an inclination of $i\simeq 107^{\circ}$, where i is the angle between the orbital angular momentum and the line of sight. The top panel shows the corresponding plus-polarization strain $h_{+}(t)$, and the middle panel shows the instantaneous GW frequency, with markers indicating where the signal reaches the BAYESTAR cutoff frequencies of 29, 38, 56, and 1024 Hz (approximately 51, 25, and 9 s before merger, and at merger). The lower panels show the BAYESTAR sky maps generated at each cutoff, which evolve from broad and multimodal at early times to compact near merger; the dot marks the posterior maximum.

Figure 2: 
Example paired rollouts comparing the RL policy with the visibility-aware peak-tracking baseline. In each row, the left panel shows the earliest BAYESTAR map (logarithmic stretch) with the $90\%$ credible contours of all four localization stages, the dashed curve marks the $20^{\circ}$ minimum-elevation boundary, with the inaccessible sky below it shaded. The pointing trajectories of the two controllers are colored by episode time, and the right panel zooms in on the final localization. Top row: an arc-like localization in which both controllers reach the dominant mode, and the RL trajectory remains slightly better aligned with the broader posterior structure, yielding a capture reward a few percent above the baseline. Bottom row: an event whose pre-merger posterior maxima are noticeably offset from the eventual source position; the peak-tracking controller follows these offset maxima and is still approaching the source at merger, while the learned policy settles onto it earlier and accumulates roughly $40\%$ more capture reward, mostly in the heavily weighted post-merger window.

Figure 3: GW170817-like localization evolution for a two-detector Hanford–Livingston network with Virgo removed (top block) and a three-detector Hanford–Livingston–Virgo network (bottom block), for the same injection and localization pipeline. Panels show the BAYESTAR sky maps at the 29, 38, 56, and 1024 Hz frequency cutoffs. The star marks the true source position and the dot the posterior maximum. With three detectors the maximum coincides with the true position from the earliest map, whereas the two-detector posterior is an extended arc whose maximum lies tens of degrees from the source until shortly before merger.

Figure 4: Prototype Deep Synoptic Array (DSA) antennas at the Owens Valley Radio Observatory. The test array includes multiple prototype antenna generations developed as part of the DSA program. The two leftmost antennas in this image were used for the trajectory-playback tests presented in this work. These tests provide a pathfinder validation of rapid follow-up operations, including antenna repointing, slew-time constraints, and the interface between optimized pointing policies and real telescope control. Credit: Vinand Prayag.

Figure 5: Prototype DSA antenna executing one of the simulated GW follow-up trajectories through the programmed-track interface. Top: commanded (dashed) and achieved (solid, encoder telemetry) azimuth and elevation. The commanded curve is the precomputed trajectory supplied to the antenna controller. Bottom: total sky-plane offset between the achieved pointing and the requested trajectory (red), and the drive’s internal servo error, i.e. the achieved position relative to the controller’s own smoothed setpoint (grey); the dotted line marks the primary-beam half width at half maximum (HWHM, $1.25\arcdeg$). The difference between the two curves is due to the drive’s internal trajectory shaping rather than to servo-following error: the commanded ramps are delayed by $\sim$0.9 s on the elevation axis and $\sim$0.1 s in azimuth, producing the initial plateau while both axes ramp, the $\sim$$0.1\arcdeg$ floor during the remaining azimuth ramp, and the brief excursions at the elevation steps. The curves coincide once the commanded rates drop to zero.

Figure 6: Architecture of the explored pointing framework, including an optional classifier-based dispatch stage. Top: the pre-merger dispatch stage summarizes the earliest BAYESTAR map into five features, and a random-forest classifier routes most alerts to the visibility-aware peak-tracking controller, while sending selected alerts predicted to benefit from the learned policy to the RL controller. Bottom: the RL pointing policy. BAYESTAR maps and the telescope state are converted into a fixed observation (projected sky-map channels, scalar features, recent history), processed by separate map, vector, and history encoders, and passed to a shared actor–critic network; the actor outputs a bounded slew command and the environment updates the pointing, visibility, coverage, and reward. The critic and PPO update are used only during training.

Figure 7: Classifier-gated performance as the routing threshold is varied over an exploratory held-out set of approximately $10^{3}$ paired test cases. Each test case consists of one simulated event evaluated at a particular observing time and initial telescope pointing. For each classifier threshold, the lower horizontal axis gives the fraction of test cases with $P_{\rm win}$ above that threshold and therefore routed to RL; the upper axis gives the corresponding empirical $P_{\rm win}$ threshold. The upper panel shows the aggregate post-merger capture-score change relative to peak tracking within the routed subset, and the lower panel shows the fractions of RL wins, numerical ties, and peak-tracking wins. At $P_{\rm win}\geq 0.65$, approximately $2\%$ of test cases are routed to RL, yielding a $3.15\%$ aggregate improvement.

2610.40958.abstract: Prompt millisecond-duration coherent radio emission is proposed as a counterpart to neutron-star-containing compact mergers, produced before, during, or shortly after coalescence. Its detection would probe the plasma environment, magnetic fields, remnant evolution, and emission physics of these mergers. At GHz frequencies, dispersive delays can range from fractions of a second to several seconds, requiring the telescope to be on source before or soon after coalescence. Negative- or low-latency alerts, rapid response, and optimized pointing under uncertain, evolving localizations are therefore essential. We present a framework for prompt gravitational-wave follow-up with the upcoming Deep Synoptic Array (DSA), a sensitive, fast-slewing, wide-field GHz radio array. We simulate low-latency localization sequences and embed them in a follow-up environment with elevation, field-of-view, and slew constraints. We compare a reinforcement-learning pointing policy with a baseline that slews toward the highest-probability accessible region at each step. This peak-tracking rule is a strong, interpretable baseline for initial deployment, while the learned policy provides a complementary strategy for a subset of broad, multimodal, or arc-shaped localizations. At a random merger time, 37% of events are observable above $20^\circ$ elevation; among these, $\sim90\%$ of BNS events are successfully reached and tracked using zero-noise localization maps, decreasing to $\sim75\%$ with Gaussian-noise maps. We validate the optimized pointing trajectories on prototype DSA antennas. DSA follow-up can reach a fluence sensitivity of $\sim20$ mJy ms over a representative 700-1025 MHz sub-band, probing millisecond bursts with luminosities of approximately $10^{38}$ to $10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$, at or below the lower end of several coherent-emission predictions for neutron-star mergers.

2610.41119.title: MAGIKS: Multimodal Alignment and Gravitational-Wave-Conditioned Interaction for Kilonova Search

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed multimodal framework for gravitational-wave-triggered kilonova counterpart search. The upper stream encodes the gravitational-wave trigger using source-parameter descriptors and the sky-localization map: scalar parameters are projected with a multilayer perceptron (MLP), while the skymap is processed by a one-dimensional convolutional network and pooled into a localization feature. The lower stream encodes Rubin/LSST optical alerts using irregularly sampled multiband light curves and sky coordinates: temporal samples are represented on a reference time grid with time embeddings and encoded by the Multi-Time Attention Network (mTAN) module, while coordinates are encoded separately. The contrastive-learning branch projects the gravitational-wave and optical representations into a shared embedding space and uses a supervised contrastive objective with a time-compatibility term to favour physically plausible pairs. The fusion branch performs two explicit cross-modal matching operations, comparing optical coordinates with the gravitational-wave localization and gravitational-wave source descriptors with the optical temporal evolution, and produces the final ranking score for counterpart retrieval.

Figure 2: Sampled component-mass distributions for the BNS test set. The double-Gaussian distribution of recycled neutron stars (blue) is from N. Farrow et al. [22], and the distribution of slowly rotating neutron stars (red) is from S. Galaudage et al. [25]. Both components are truncated to the neutron-star mass range used in this work.

Figure 3: Joint distribution of sampled component masses for the NSBH test set. The central panel shows the two-dimensional distribution of neutron-star mass $m_{\rm NS}$ and black-hole mass $m_{\rm BH}$, with colour indicating the probability per hexagonal bin. The top and right panels show the distributions of neutron stars (NS) and black holes (BH) separately. The BH mass axis is logarithmic.

Figure 4: Empirical probability-density distributions of the delay between the gravitational-wave trigger time and the first retained LSST detection in the training–validation dataset. The blue curve shows the baseline light curves, the red curve shows the light curves with ToO follow-up, and the shaded gray curve shows their combined distribution. ToO follow-up is applied to 45.9% of the positive gravitational-wave events and contributes 89.6% of the retained light curves. The median delays are 1.43 days for Baseline, 0.56 days for ToO follow-up, and 0.60 days for the combined sample.

Figure 5: Representative kilonova and non-kilonova light curves in luptitude space after Rubin-style sampling and preprocessing. Panels (a)–(c) show typical kilonova light curves under the Baseline, Gold, and Silver observation strategies, respectively, while panels (d)–(f) show representative supernova, tidal disruption event, and active galactic nucleus contaminants, respectively. Different colours denote the LSST $ugrizY$ bands, and the horizontal axis is measured relative to the first optical detection. Open circles represent non-detected observations, while filled circles represent detected observations. A detection is defined as having a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of at least 5.

Figure 6: Retrieval performance as a function of gallery size for the single-modality baselines, the reproduced Fink random forest, multimodal ablations, and MAGI$K$S. Each gallery contains one true kilonova counterpart and time- and sky-compatible distractor transients. Panels (a), (b), and (c) show Recall@1, Recall@10, and mean reciprocal rank (MRR), respectively. Recall@K measures the fraction of queries for which the true counterpart is ranked within the top K candidates, while MRR measures the average inverse rank of the true counterpart. Metrics are averaged over ten independently sampled galleries for each query and gallery size.

Figure 7: Redshift dependence of retrieval performance for the single-modality baselines, the reproduced Fink random forest, multimodal ablations, and MAGIKS. Positive-query GW events populate four redshift bins, $[0.00,0.04)$, $[0.04,0.065)$, $[0.065,0.10)$, and $[0.10,0.14)$; the plotted values are the mean redshifts of the contributing queries, approximately 0.026, 0.052, 0.081, and 0.102. Panels (a), (b), and (c) show logarithmically weighted macro Recall@1, macro Recall@10, and macro MRR across the six evaluated gallery sizes.

Figure 8: Classification-logit distributions for matched positive pairs and three negative-pair categories. Optical-negative pairs combine a positive GW event with a non-KN transient, GW-negative pairs combine an optical candidate with an ejecta-free or optically undetected merger, and mismatched pairs combine a positive GW event with a KN light curve generated for another merger. Larger logits indicate stronger support for an associated pair.

Figure 9: Row-normalized confusion matrices for MAGIKS pairwise classification of BNS and NSBH systems. The positive class contains associated GW–KN pairs, and the negative class combines optical-negative, GW-negative, and mismatched pairs.

Figure 10: Directional consistency rates for MAGIKS, the physics-informed empirical bridge, and the GW-independent optical control in the single-parameter crossed-pair experiment. Points show the primary 0.5-interquartile-range caliper estimates, and error bars give 95% intervals from 10,000 bootstrap samples. The vertical dashed line marks the GW-independent value of 0.5. Detector-frame chirp mass, mass ratio, inclination, and luminosity distance are averaged with equal weight over BNS and NSBH sources. Primary black-hole spin is evaluated for NSBH systems, for which the ejecta prescription is spin dependent.

2610.41119.abstract: We present MAGIKS, a multimodal framework for gravitational-wave (GW)-triggered kilonova identification that formulates counterpart search as query-conditioned gallery retrieval. Following an align-before-fuse design, MAGIKS combines GW source parameters and sky-localization maps with irregularly sampled multiband optical light curves and sky coordinates. A time-aware supervised contrastive objective provides coarse cross-modal alignment, while dual cross-attention evaluates consistency between optical coordinates and GW localization, and between GW parameters and optical evolution. We train and evaluate MAGIKS on simulated binary neutron star and neutron star-black hole mergers, Rubin Observatory kilonova light curves from regular survey observations and target-of-opportunity follow-up, GW-detected mergers without Rubin-detectable kilonova counterparts, and realistic non-kilonova contaminants. In independent galleries with one true counterpart and time- and sky-compatible distractors, MAGIKS outperforms optical-only and sky-localization-only ranking, with increasing gains as galleries grow. At 5000 candidates, it ranks the counterpart first for 39.8% of queries, versus 4.8% and 0.2% for these baselines. In a GW170817 study, we generate counterfactual Rubin observations using released GW parameters and three-dimensional localization, the measured counterpart position, and host distance. At the same gallery size, MAGIKS achieves top-1 and top-10 retrieval rates of 87.3% and 95.7%. It correctly classifies 94.2% of associated and non-associated GW-optical pairs. In a separate crossed-pair experiment, its matching score responds significantly to controlled changes in all five tested GW parameters. These results support GW-conditioned kilonova candidate prioritisation for future multi-messenger follow-up.

2610.41229.title: More Eccentric, Not Always Less Detectable: High Mass Holds Its Ground, Low Mass Loses Reach

figures.caption:
Figure 1: 
Illustrative figure of a strain of a highly eccentric waveform as a function of time.
In addition to the usual evolution from inspiral (early time) to merger (late time),
the 
GW in the inspiral has peaks and troughs during the close and far encounters
in the orbital configuration (see top for illustration).
Consequently, highly eccentric waveforms may be amplified such that parts of the waveform
inspiral have high signal-to-noise ratio peaks, among other signatures.
The waveform morphology is very distinct from quasicircular orbits and may be missed should
incorrect templates be used.

Figure 2: 
Match between eccentric and $$q$$uasicircular gravitational waveforms, used as a preliminary estimate of
the fractional loss in optimal matched-filter 
SNR when eccentric signals are recovered with quasicircular templates.
The match is evaluated by varying the eccentricity together with one additional source parameter at a time,
while keeping the remaining parameters fixed:
chirp mass $\mathcal{M}_{c}$ (top-left),
mass ratio q with $m_{1}=5M_{\odot}$ (top-right),
mass ratio q with $m_{1}=30M_{\odot}$ (bottom-right), and
true anomaly $\zeta$ for a $30-30M_{\odot}$ binary (bottom-left).
Here the mass ratio is defined as $q=m_{2}/m_{1}$.
Unless otherwise specified by the varied parameter in each panel, the component masses are fixed to $30-30M_{\odot}$.
The yellow dashed contours indicate the $\mathcal{M}=0.97$ threshold, corresponding to a $3\%$ mismatch;
the contours are smoothed using a polynomial-regression fit.
The legend in each panel gives the parameter combination at which the minimum match occurs.
These results indicate that eccentricity is one of the dominant parameters controlling the loss in match,
with the strongest loss occurring for high eccentricity, lower chirp mass, and nearly equal-mass systems.

Figure 3: 
Illustration of the autocorrelation-based signal-consistency test used in GstLAL.
The upper panel shows the time-domain plus polarization for
equal-mass $$12$$–$12\,M_{\odot}$ waveforms, with the waveform peak aligned at $t=0$.
The grey dashed curve is the quasicircular signal, while the coloured curves show an eccentric TEOBResumS-Dalí signal with
eccentricity $e_{\rm 15Hz}=0.6$.
The blue portion indicates the part of the eccentric waveform within the signal-consistency $\xi^{2}$ time window,
while the red portion indicates the part outside this window;
the inset zooms into the waveform close to merger.
The lower panel shows the corresponding noiseless, 
PSD-weighted matched-filter 
SNR time series obtained by
sliding a quasicircular 12–$12\,M_{\odot}$ template across each injection.
The 
SNR peaks are aligned at zero lag, and the vertical dotted lines mark
the $\pm 85.4\,{\rm ms}$ window used in the signal-consistency $\xi^{2}$ calculation.
The quasicircular signal gives a normalized signal-consistency statistic $\xi^{2}/\rho^{2}=2.09\times 10^{-34}$,
while the eccentric signal gives $\xi^{2}/\rho^{2}=2.84\times 10^{-3}$,
showing that eccentricity can produce measurable deviations from the expected template autocorrelation
within the merger-centred signal-consistency-test window.

Figure 4: 
Dependence of the normalized signal-consistency-test statistic $\xi^{2}/\rho^{2}$
on chirp mass and eccentricity.
The signal-consistency $\xi^{2}$ test is used to weed out
non-Gaussian noise transients that can mimic 
GW,
but it can also be sensitive to unmodeled residual
waveform differences between the true signal (e.g., eccentric waveform strain)
and the waveform template (quasi-circular waveform strain).
The signal-consistency statistic $\xi^{2}$ is calculated by comparing
the matched-filter 
SNR time series with
the expected autocorrelation structure of the template.
We normalize the signal-consistency statistic $\xi^{2}$ by the square of the optimal 
SNR,
$\rho^{2}$, to measure the residual strength relative to the signal strength.
The results indicate that eccentricity has little effect on the normalized signal-consistency statistic $\xi^{2}/\rho^{2}$
for higher chirp masses,
while the statistic increases with eccentricity for lower chirp masses,
especially below $\mathcal{M}_{c}\sim 20\,M_{\odot}$.

Figure 5: 
Recovery results for injection campaign 1, using $$30$$–$30\,M_{\odot}$
eccentric injections with randomized eccentricity.
The panels show the recovered network 
SNR $\rho$ (left),
normalized signal-consistency-test statistic $\xi^{2}/\rho^{2}$ (middle), and
false alarm rate (right) as functions of eccentricity.
The normalized signal-consistency $\xi^{2}/\rho^{2}$ panel is shown on a logarithmic scale.
The recovered 
FAR and 
SNR show no clear monotonic degradation with
increasing eccentricity; a straight-line fit to
$\log_{10}(\mathrm{FAR})$ (dashed line, right panel)
has a slope of $-0.66$, negligible against the scatter,
confirming the absence of a 
FAR trend with eccentricity.
The right panel is restricted to the main low-
FAR population.
The normalized signal-consistency statistic $\xi^{2}/\rho^{2}$ increases mildly
with eccentricity but gradually flattens at higher eccentricities,
indicating that eccentricity has only a small effect on the signal-consistency test
and does not lead to a significant loss in search sensitivity for this
30–$30\,M_{\odot}$ configuration.

Figure 6: 
Recovered-trigger distribution for the fixed-eccentricity injection sets at $$30$$–$30\,M_{\odot}$.
Each panel corresponds to one eccentricity value, generated with TEOBResumS-Dalí: $e_{\rm 15Hz}=0$, $0.2$, $0.4$, $0.6$, $0.8$, and $0.99$.
The horizontal axis shows the recovered 
SNR $\rho$, while the vertical axis shows the normalized signal-consistency-test statistic $\xi^{2}/\rho^{2}$.
The colour scale indicates the 
FAR of the recovered trigger.
Across all eccentricity values, the recovered injections occupy a similar region in the recovered-SNR–normalized-signal-consistency ($\rho$–$\xi^{2}/\rho^{2}$) plane, indicating that increasing eccentricity does not produce a clear degradation in recovered 
SNR or signal consistency for this 30–$30\,M_{\odot}$ configuration.

Figure 7: 
Recovery results for injection campaign 3,
using $$12$$–$12\,M_{\odot}$ eccentric injections with randomized eccentricity.
The panels show the recovered network 
SNR $\rho$ (left),
normalized signal-consistency-test statistic $\xi^{2}/\rho^{2}$ (middle), and
false alarm rate (right) as functions of eccentricity.
The normalized signal-consistency $\xi^{2}/\rho^{2}$ panel is shown on a logarithmic scale.
The recovered injections show no clear monotonic degradation
in 
FAR or 
SNR with increasing eccentricity;
a straight-line fit to $\log_{10}(\mathrm{FAR})$ (dashed line, right panel)
has a slope of $+0.06$, consistent with zero within the scatter.
The right panel is restricted to the main low-
FAR population.
The normalized signal-consistency statistic $\xi^{2}/\rho^{2}$ shows only a very weak increasing
trend with eccentricity, indicating that eccentricity has a small effect on the
signal-consistency test but does not significantly affect the recovery or
search sensitivity for this 12–$12\,M_{\odot}$ configuration.

Figure 8: 
Recovered-trigger distributions for injection campaign 4,
using fixed-eccentricity $12$–$12\,M_{\odot}$ injection sets.
Each panel corresponds to one eccentricity value:
$e_{\rm 15Hz}=0$, $0.2$, $0.4$, $0.6$, $0.8$, and $0.99$.
The horizontal axis shows the recovered 
SNR $\rho$,
while the vertical axis shows the normalized signal-consistency-test statistic $\xi^{2}/\rho^{2}$.
The colour scale indicates the 
FAR of the recovered triggers.
The recovered-trigger distributions remain broadly similar across eccentricity values,
indicating that increasing eccentricity does not produce a clear systematic degradation
in recovered 
SNR, signal consistency, or 
FAR for this lower-mass configuration.

Figure 9: 
Average recovered network 
SNR $\langle\rho\rangle$ as a function of eccentricity for
the $30$–$30\,M_{\odot}$ (left, injection campaign 1) and
$12$–$12\,M_{\odot}$ (right, injection campaign 3) configurations.
Each point is the mean recovered 
SNR in an eccentricity bin, and
the blue dotted line marks the estimated injected 
SNR.
The error bars quantify the uncertainty in the mean recovered 
SNR
after accounting for the antenna response and
the modeled detector effects;
they do not include a correction for waveform mismatch,
which can only systematically reduce the recovered 
SNR.
The horizontal line therefore represents a reference mean,
not an upper limit on the recovered 
SNR:
bin averages may lie above or below it because the injection samples and detector responses differ,
and the error bars quantify the uncertainty in each recovered mean rather than the
expected difference from the reference.
A deficit relative to the reference provides evidence for mismatch,
subject to the accuracy of the reference and the uncertainty model.

Figure 10: 
Time-domain plus polarization $h_{+}$ of a representative eccentric injection compared with
two quasicircular templates, aligned at the amplitude peak.
In both panels the pink solid curve is the eccentric injection ($$e=0$.25$) and
the blue dashed curve is a quasicircular (e=0) template.
Upper panel: the best-matching template found by the search,
whose intrinsic parameters
($m_{1}=36.565\,M_{\odot}$, $m_{2}=24.831\,M_{\odot}$, $\chi_{1z}=0.560$, $\chi_{2z}=-0.990$)
differ from those of the injection; it achieves a match of $\mathcal{M}=0.9381$.
Lower panel: a quasicircular template with the same source parameters as the injection
(except for zero eccentricity), which achieves a lower match, $\mathcal{M}=0.9108$.
Because the search maximizes over the whole template bank, it recovers the eccentric signal
with the higher-overlap best-matching template rather than the same-source quasicircular one,
which is why the recovered 
SNR can exceed
a same-source reference (Figure 9).

2610.41229.abstract: Gravitational waves from eccentric compact binary coalescences trace dynamical binary formation, but matched-filtering searches responsible for most detections rely on quasicircular templates. Quantifying any sensitivity loss is crucial for assessing population completeness and the need for dedicated eccentric template banks. We present the first systematic GstLAL search study spanning eccentricities up to $e_{\rm 15Hz}=0.99$ and broad ranges of chirp mass, mass ratio, inclination, and aligned spin. Using TEOBResumS-Dalí waveforms, we inject eccentric signals and measure recovered signal-to-noise ratio, signal-consistency statistics, false-alarm rate, and sensitive volume and distance. For high-mass binaries ($\mathcal{M}_c\gtrsim30\,M_\odot$), sensitive distance is nearly independent of eccentricity, demonstrating that greater eccentricity does not necessarily reduce search sensitivity. In contrast, for low-mass binaries, sensitive distance falls by up to $\sim50\%$ near $e_{\rm 15Hz}\approx0.75$. Although the absolute loss in reach is modest given their low quasicircular sensitivity, this relative reduction exceeds the increase in sensitive distance between the second and third observing runs of the LIGO--Virgo--KAGRA collaboration and is consistent with previous low-mass studies. We also find that waveform matches at fixed source parameters substantially overpredict search sensitivity loss, meaning that the pipeline's signal-consistency test and maximization over its template bank mitigate much of the predicted sensitivity loss. This highlights the need for end-to-end injection campaigns to establish the detectability of eccentric binaries.

2610.41252.title: The Effect of Large Apertures on Atmospheric Noise Spectra for Millimeter-wave Telescopes

figures.caption: Figure 1: Modeled atmospheric map noise spectra from our toy model, computed from Equation 16, for different primary diameters $D$. All other parameters take the value specified in Table 1. The black solid curve is the lensed CMB temperature power spectrum, and the grey horizontal line indicates the white noise level at 150 GHz for a fiducial 5-year survey. The dotted line shows the standard power-law approximation for the atmosphere, normalized to the $D=10$ m curve at $\ell=100$, where beam effects are negligible. We see that for large apertures, the atmospheric noise can be significantly lower than the standard power-law assumption.

Figure 2: Same as Figure 1, but fixing the primary aperture $D=10$ m and varying the scale height $h_{0}$, which parameterizes the vertical decay length of atmospheric fluctuations; $\sigma_{\rho,\text{base}}$ is rescaled to keep $\langle\delta w^{2}\rangle$ fixed (see Section IV.2). The dotted line is the power-law approximation, normalized to the fiducial curve at $\ell=100$. We see that increasing the scale height raises the atmospheric spectrum, most strongly at high $\ell$.

Figure 3: Same as Figure 2, but varying the outer scale $r_{0}$, which is the characteristic correlation length of turbulent fluctuations. Increasing $r_{0}$ lowers the atmospheric spectrum by an overall factor without changing its shape.

2610.41252.abstract: Ground-based millimeter and submillimeter telescopes produce astronomical maps that contain a combination of noise inherent to themselves as well as contamination from foregrounds, with the strongest foreground being fluctuating atmospheric emission. While the emission of the turbulent atmosphere itself follows a scale-free power law, the atmosphere as seen by the telescope is modified by the properties of the instrument optics. A naive power-law extrapolation of the atmospheric noise spectrum ignores the blurring effect of the near-field beam, which becomes more pronounced for larger telescope apertures and at higher multipoles. In this work, we use a toy model to derive a semianalytic estimate of the atmospheric noise spectrum that takes into account the effects of near-field optics. We show that it has an appreciable effect for large-aperture telescopes, suggesting that ultra-sensitive, high-resolution experiments are not necessarily limited by the atmosphere on small angular scales. We also present an estimate of the atmospheric knee as a function of the primary aperture, the atmospheric scale height, and the outer scale of turbulence.

2610.41412.title: Conceptual Design of a Compact Magnetic Spectrometer for Space Radiation Measurement

figures.caption: Figure 1: The timeline and energy coverage of recent experiments measuring high-energy fluxes of charged particles in LEO. This work proposes a magnetic spectrometer, COMIRA, to investigate a unique energy range from tens of MeV to several GeV.
Figure 3: The geometrical acceptance of the compact magnetic spectrometer for electrons and positrons (red), protons (magenta), helium (blue) and oxygen (black).
Figure 4: The rigidity resolution as a function of generated rigidity for electrons (red), protons (pink), helium (blue) and oxygen (black). As seen, the maximum detectable rigidity is $\sim 5$ GV.
Figure 5: The velocity resolution of reconstructed with TOF as a function of generated rigidity for electrons (red), protons (pink), and helium (blue).

Figure 7: The charge sign confusion ratio of electrons, which are misidentified as positrons from the velocity direction and bending curvature. The charge confusion ratio is $<10^{-3}$ for rigidities from 8 MV to 1.3 GV.

Figure 8: The proton rejection at $95\textrm{\%}$ positron efficiency as a function of rigidity using the $\beta_{\textrm{TOF}}$ + $\Delta E/\Delta x$ cut (blue), and with additional cut on $N^{\textrm{TCC}}_{\textrm{p.e.}}$ (pink).

2610.41412.abstract: We present the design of COMIRA, a compact magnetic spectrometer for space radiation measurement. The spectrometer consists of four layers of scintillating fiber trackers, four layers of silicon strip trackers, one threshold Cherenkov counter, two anti-coincidence counters, and a permanent magnet. The detector has an overall dimension of approximately 12x12 cm3 and a geometrical acceptance of ~6.6 cm2sr. Based on combined measurements of charge, velocity, and rigidity (momentum/charge), it enables the simultaneous measurement of the energy spectrum, angular distribution and time evolution of individual radiation components, including electrons, positrons, protons and light nuclei over an energy range from tens of MeV to several GeV. The design can be further optimized depending on the available resources and constraints of the hosting space platform.

2610.42009.abstract:
We trained a convolutional neural network to detect ultra-short-period planets in TESS photometry, following the procedure now standard in the field: synthetic transits as positives, eclipsing binaries as negatives. Measured that way it reaches an area under the ROC curve of 0.97. Keeping the same model and the same planets, but replacing the negatives with false positives that the TESS Follow-up Observing Program has actually rejected, the area falls to 0.50 -- the value of a random classifier. The conventional benchmark had been measuring a problem that does not exist.
The reason is physical, and it bounds what is possible. Of 145 such false positives examined at pixel level, 42% are blends: eclipses belonging to a neighbouring star, diluted into the target aperture. Their light curves are indistinguishable from shallow transits, capping the attainable area at 1 - f/2 = 0.79. Retraining on real false positives reaches 0.80 +/- 0.06, confirming the ceiling independently. No classifier reading a single-band light curve can do better.
A detector alone is the wrong instrument. We built CASCADE-USP, a pipeline chaining the network with difference-image centroid analysis, scene modelling with high-resolution imaging and the Gaia astrometric solution, supplying in sequence what the light curve lacks. Its output is a prioritisation, not a verdict: it records what evidence each candidate still needs. Only the classifier is domain-specific; the other stages apply to any transit candidate. Of 435 unresolved TESS candidates it isolates 20; 19 prove false positives, traced to causes invisible in TESS photometry. The twentieth is TOI-6662 b, an Earth-sized planet (0.94 +/- 0.03 Earth radii) orbiting an M dwarf every 7.05 hours. Our validation, independent of a concurrent one, agrees with it in planetary parameters and classification, closing the CASCADE procedure with an external check.

2610.42035.title: Distinguishing N$_2$-Dominated from O$_2$-Dominated Atmospheres on Terrestrial Exoplanets with Reflected-Light Spectroscopy

2610.42035.abstract: Reflected-light spectra of Earth-sized exoplanets promise to probe habitability and biosignatures, but interpreting atmospheric oxygen can be challenging because $O_2$ can arise from both biological and abiotic processes. In addition, reflected-light retrievals exhibit degeneracies among atmospheric composition, clouds, surface reflectance, and gravity. We use the Bayesian retrieval framework ExoReL$^\Re$, leveraging recent model developments that incorporate (i) $O_2$-$O_2$ collision-induced absorption (CIA), which produces the $O_4$ bands, and (ii) a wavelength-dependent (step-function) surface albedo parameterization. Focusing on a modern Earth analog, we compare retrievals with and without $O_2$-$O_2$ CIA using spectra within 0.25-1.8 $\mu$m, and perform signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) sweeps for two observing configurations motivated by the Habitable Worlds Observatory: a resolved-visible case ($R_{VIS}=140$) and a broadband-visible case (three broad bins). Omitting $O_2$-$O_2$ CIA allows the retrieval to fit the spectrum with an incorrect $O_2$-dominated atmosphere. Including $O_2$-$O_2$ CIA leverages the $O_4$ bands to break this degeneracy and recover the correct $N_2$-dominated, $O_2$-rich solution without requiring a tight mass prior. Adopting a robustness criterion of $\ge95\%$ posterior mass in the $N_2$-dominated region, both configurations require SNR $\gtrsim20$ at 0.75 $\mu$m (SNR $\approx14$ near the 1.27 $\mu$m $O_4$ band for $R_{NIR}=70$) to identify the correct dominant gas, with higher cloud fraction increasing this threshold. Reducing near-IR coverage to 1.4 $\mu$m prevents recovery of the correct $N_2$-dominated solution across the explored SNR range, and instead favors a spurious $O_2$-dominated, $CO_2$-rich atmosphere. These results support near-IR coverage to $\sim1.7$ $\mu$m and SNR $\gtrsim20$ at 0.75 $\mu$m for robust oxygen interpretation on Earth-like planets.
